statement: Let $X$ be the [projective limit](c:limit-category-theory) of a projective system of [Hausdorff spaces](c:hausdorff-space) $Y_j$ over a directed set $J$, with projections $p_j$. Let $\mu_\varepsilon$ be Borel [probability measures](c:probability-measure) on $X$ whose pushforwards to each $Y_j$ satisfy a [large deviation principle](c:large-deviation-principle) with a good [rate function](c:rate-function) $I_j$. Then $\mu_\varepsilon$ satisfies it with the good rate function $I(x) = \sup_j I_j(p_j(x))$.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is the [projective limit](c:limit-category-theory) of a projective system $(Y_j, p_{ij})_{j \in J}$ of [Hausdorff spaces](c:hausdorff-space) over a directed set $J$.
The $\mu_\varepsilon$, for $\varepsilon > 0$, are Borel [probability measures](c:probability-measure) on $X$.
For each $j$, the pushforwards $\mu_\varepsilon \circ p_j^{-1}$ satisfy a [large deviation principle](c:large-deviation-principle) with a good [rate function](c:rate-function) $I_j$.

conclusion: The family $\mu_\varepsilon$ satisfies a [large deviation principle](c:large-deviation-principle) with the good rate function $I(x) = \sup_j I_j(p_j(x))$.

proofs.name: Compact level sets and compatible projections
proofs.slogan: Check both bounds on the projections, and use compact level sets to pass to the limit.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, where the principle means the upper bound on closed sets and the lower bound on open sets as $\varepsilon \to 0$, with compact level sets. The index set $J$ is nonempty and directed.

roles.why: Directedness makes the pulled-back open sets a base, and the Hausdorff property makes $X$ closed in the product and level sets compact.
The measure of a set $p_j^{-1}(U)$ equals the pushforward measure of $U$.
The bounds for each $I_j$ transfer to the sets $p_j^{-1}(U)$ and $p_j^{-1}(F_j)$ of $X$.

steps.slogan: Describe the open and closed sets of $X$ through the projections $p_j$.
steps.detail: Since $J$ is directed, the sets $p_j^{-1}(U)$ with $U$ open in $Y_j$ are closed under finite intersections, so they form a base of $X$. Hence a closed set $F$ satisfies $F = \bigcap_j p_j^{-1}(F_j)$ with $F_j = \overline{p_j(F)}$: a point $x \notin F$ has a basic neighborhood $p_j^{-1}(U)$ missing $F$, so $p_j(x) \notin F_j$.

steps.slogan: Prove the lower bound on basic open sets and take the supremum.
steps.detail: Let $G$ be open and $x \in G$. Choose $j$ and an open $U$ with $x \in p_j^{-1}(U) \subseteq G$. The lower bound for $\mu_\varepsilon \circ p_j^{-1}$ gives $\liminf \varepsilon \log \mu_\varepsilon(G) \ge -\inf_U I_j \ge -I_j(p_j(x)) \ge -I(x)$; now take the supremum over $x \in G$.

steps.slogan: Show that $I$ is lower semicontinuous with compact level sets.
steps.detail: Each $I_j \circ p_j$ is [lower semicontinuous](c:lower-semicontinuity), so their supremum $I$ is too. For $\alpha \ge 0$ the set $K_j = \{I_j \le \alpha\}$ is [compact](c:compact-space), and $\{I \le \alpha\} = X \cap \prod_j K_j$. The product is compact by Tychonoff's theorem and $X$ is closed in $\prod_j Y_j$ because the $Y_j$ are Hausdorff, so the level set is compact.

steps.slogan: Show that the rate functions are compatible: $I_j(p_{jk}(y)) \le I_k(y)$ for $j \le k$.
steps.detail: Fix $j \le k$, $y \in Y_k$ and an open $U \ni p_{jk}(y)$. Since $\mu_\varepsilon(p_j^{-1}U) = \mu_\varepsilon(p_k^{-1}(p_{jk}^{-1}U))$, the lower bound on $Y_k$ gives $\liminf \varepsilon \log \mu_\varepsilon(p_j^{-1}U) \ge -I_k(y)$. If $I_j(p_{jk}(y)) > a > I_k(y)$, choose $U$ with $\overline U$ missing the compact set $\{I_j \le a\}$ (Hausdorff); the upper bound on $\overline U$ gives $\limsup \le -a$, a contradiction.

steps.slogan: Bound a closed set $F$ by the closed sets $p_j^{-1}(F_j)$ that contain it.
steps.detail: Because $F \subseteq p_j^{-1}(F_j)$, the upper bound on $Y_j$ gives $\limsup \varepsilon \log \mu_\varepsilon(F) \le -\inf_{F_j} I_j$ for every $j$. So it suffices to show $\sup_j \inf_{F_j} I_j \ge \inf_F I$.

steps.slogan: Build a point of $F$ with small rate from compact sets that fit together.
steps.detail: Suppose $\sup_j \inf_{F_j} I_j < \alpha < \inf_F I$. Then $C_j = F_j \cap \{I_j \le \alpha\}$ is nonempty and compact, and $p_{jk}(C_k) \subseteq C_j$ by continuity and the compatibility step. A projective limit of nonempty compact Hausdorff spaces over a directed set is nonempty, so some $x \in X$ has $p_j(x) \in C_j$ for all $j$. Then $x \in F$ and $I(x) \le \alpha$, against $\alpha < \inf_F I$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two bounds and the compact level sets into the principle.
steps.detail: The lower bound for open sets, the upper bound for closed sets and the compact level sets of $I$ are exactly the statement that $\mu_\varepsilon$ satisfies the large deviation principle with the good rate function $I$.

concepts.c:limit-category-theory: The limit carries the coarsest topology that makes every projection $p_j$ continuous.
concepts.c:hausdorff-space: Hausdorff spaces separate a point from a compact set and make compact sets closed.
concepts.c:probability-measure: The pushforwards of the measures $\mu_\varepsilon$ to the spaces $Y_j$ carry the hypothesis.
concepts.c:large-deviation-principle: The proof checks its upper bound on closed sets and lower bound on open sets.
concepts.c:rate-function: The rate function $I$ is built as a supremum of the rate functions $I_j$.
concepts.c:lower-semicontinuity: Lower semicontinuity survives suprema, so $I$ is lower semicontinuous.
concepts.c:compact-space: Compact level sets of the $I_j$ give compact level sets of $I$.

source.note: The statement is Dembo and Zeitouni, Large Deviations Techniques and Applications, 2nd ed., Theorem 4.6.1; the proof is written out directly from the definitions.

statement: Let $\psi = \Gamma'/\Gamma$ be the [digamma function](c:digamma-function), the logarithmic derivative of the [Gamma function](c:gamma-function). For every complex $s$ with $2s \notin \{0, -1, -2, \dots\}$, $\psi(2s) = \tfrac12\big(\psi(s) + \psi(s + \tfrac12)\big) + \log 2$.

hypotheses.text: The complex number $s$ satisfies $2s \ne -m$ for every integer $m \ge 0$.

proofs.name: Logarithmic derivative of Legendre's formula
proofs.slogan: Differentiate the logarithm of Legendre's duplication formula for the Gamma function.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for complex $s$ outside the poles, where the digamma function is defined by $\psi = \Gamma'/\Gamma$.

roles.why: It keeps $s$, $s + \tfrac12$ and $2s$ away from the poles of $\Gamma$, so every logarithmic derivative below exists.

steps.slogan: Recall Legendre's duplication formula for the [Gamma function](c:gamma-function).
steps.detail: For $z$ outside the poles, $\Gamma(z)\,\Gamma(z + \tfrac12) = 2^{1-2z}\sqrt{\pi}\,\Gamma(2z)$. It follows from $B(z,z) = 2^{1-2z}B(z,\tfrac12)$ for $\operatorname{Re} z > 0$ and extends by analytic continuation; mathlib proves it as Complex.Gamma_mul_Gamma_add_half.

steps.slogan: Show that both sides are differentiable and nonzero near $s$.
steps.detail: If $s = -m$ or $s + \tfrac12 = -m$, then $2s = -2m$ or $2s = -2m - 1$, against the hypothesis. So $\Gamma$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) at $s$, $s + \tfrac12$ and $2s$, and $\Gamma$ has no zeros, so both sides of Legendre's formula are nonzero and differentiable near $s$.

steps.slogan: Take the [logarithmic derivative](c:logarithmic-derivative) of the left side.
steps.detail: The logarithmic derivative of a product is the sum of the logarithmic derivatives. The shift $z \mapsto z + \tfrac12$ has derivative $1$, so the left side gives $\psi(s) + \psi(s + \tfrac12)$.

steps.slogan: Take the logarithmic derivative of the right side.
steps.detail: The factor $\sqrt{\pi}$ is constant. The chain rule gives $2\psi(2s)$ for $\Gamma(2z)$ and $-2\log 2$ for $2^{1-2z}$, since $\tfrac{d}{dz} 2^{1-2z} = -2\log 2 \cdot 2^{1-2z}$. So the right side gives $2\psi(2s) - 2\log 2$.

steps.slogan: Equate the two logarithmic derivatives and solve for $\psi(2s)$.
steps.detail: Legendre's formula holds for all $z$ near $s$, so the two logarithmic derivatives agree at $s$: $\psi(s) + \psi(s + \tfrac12) = 2\psi(2s) - 2\log 2$. Dividing by $2$ and rearranging gives the formula.

concepts.c:digamma-function: The digamma function is the logarithmic derivative of $\Gamma$, the object of the identity.
concepts.c:gamma-function: Legendre's formula for $\Gamma$ is the identity that the proof differentiates.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy of $\Gamma$ away from its poles allows differentiation.
concepts.c:logarithmic-derivative: Logarithmic derivatives turn products into sums and define $\psi$.

statement: Let $E$ be an exchange economy with finitely many agent types, each with a continuous, strictly monotone and strictly convex [preference relation](c:preference-relation) on $\mathbb{R}^L_+$ and a strictly positive endowment, and let $E_r$ be its $r$-fold replica. An allocation $x$ of $E$, read as an equal-treatment allocation of $E_r$, lies in the [core of the economy](c:core-of-an-economy) $E_r$ for every $r \ge 1$ if and only if it is a [Walrasian equilibrium](c:walrasian-equilibrium) allocation of $E$.

hypotheses.text: The economy $E$ has $I$ agent types and $L$ goods, type $i$ has an endowment $\omega_i \gg 0$, and $E_r$ has $r$ agents of each type.
Each [preference relation](c:preference-relation) $\succsim_i$ on $\mathbb{R}^L_+$ is continuous, strictly monotone and strictly convex.

conclusion: The allocation $x$ lies in the [core of the economy](c:core-of-an-economy) $E_r$ for all $r \ge 1$ if and only if it is a [Walrasian equilibrium](c:walrasian-equilibrium) allocation of $E$.

new_concepts.name: core of an economy
new_concepts.reminder: The set of feasible allocations that no coalition of agents can improve for all its members by trading among themselves.
new_concepts.definition: In an exchange economy, a coalition $S$ blocks a feasible allocation $x$ if its members can redistribute their own endowments into bundles $y_k$ with $y_k \succ_k x_k$ for all $k \in S$. The core is the set of feasible allocations that no coalition blocks.

proofs.name: Budget argument and separation of net trades
proofs.slogan: A budget argument keeps a Walrasian allocation in every core, and separating a convex set of preferred net trades from zero gives the price.
proofs.scope: The proof treats equal-treatment allocations, where feasible means that the bundles sum to the total endowment and a coalition blocks when all its members strictly gain; that every core allocation of $E_r$ has equal treatment is a further step of Debreu and Scarf, not proved here.

roles.why: Positive endowments give positive wealth $p \cdot \omega_i$, and replication allows coalitions with $q_i \le r$ members of each type.
Continuity makes the sets $\Gamma_i$ open, convexity makes them convex, and strict monotonicity gives positive prices.

steps.slogan: Show that a Walrasian equilibrium allocation lies in the core of every replica.
steps.detail: Let $(p, x)$ be a Walrasian equilibrium and suppose a coalition $S$ of $E_r$ blocks with bundles $y_k$. A bundle strictly preferred to $x_k$ is unaffordable, so $p \cdot y_k > p \cdot \omega_k$ for each $k \in S$. Summing gives $p \cdot \sum_S y_k > p \cdot \sum_S \omega_k$, which contradicts $\sum_S y_k = \sum_S \omega_k$.

steps.slogan: Collect the net trades that type $i$ strictly prefers into a convex set $\Gamma_i$.
steps.detail: Let $x$ lie in the core of every $E_r$ and put $\Gamma_i = \{z : \omega_i + z \succ_i x_i\}$. These sets are open by continuity, [convex](c:convex-set) because preferences are convex, and contain $x_i - \omega_i + \delta\mathbf{1}$ for every $\delta > 0$ by strict monotonicity.

steps.slogan: Show that $0$ lies outside the convex hull $\Gamma$ of the sets $\Gamma_i$.
steps.detail: Suppose $0 = \sum_i \lambda_i z_i$ with $z_i \in \Gamma_i$, $\lambda_i \ge 0$ and $\sum_i \lambda_i = 1$. Openness lets us replace the $\lambda_i$ by rationals $q_i/r$ and absorb the small error in one $z_i$. Then $q_i \le r$ agents of type $i$ can each move to $\omega_i + z_i$ within their own endowments, since $\sum_i q_i z_i = 0$, and all strictly gain, so they block $x$ in $E_r$.

steps.slogan: Separate $0$ from $\Gamma$ by a hyperplane and read its normal $p$ as a price.
steps.detail: The separating [hyperplane](c:hyperplane) theorem gives $p \ne 0$ with $p \cdot z \ge 0$ on $\Gamma$. Since $z + te_l \in \Gamma_i$ for $z \in \Gamma_i$ and $t > 0$, we get $p \ge 0$; letting $\delta \to 0$ gives $p \cdot (x_i - \omega_i) \ge 0$ for all $i$. These terms sum to $0$ by feasibility, so $p \cdot x_i = p \cdot \omega_i > 0$.

steps.slogan: Show that each $x_i$ maximizes the preference of type $i$ on its budget set.
steps.detail: Suppose $y \succ_i x_i$ and $p \cdot y \le p \cdot \omega_i$. By continuity $(1-\delta)y \succ_i x_i$ for small $\delta > 0$, so $(1-\delta)y - \omega_i \in \Gamma_i$, yet $p \cdot ((1-\delta)y - \omega_i) < 0$ because $p \cdot \omega_i > 0$. This contradicts $p \cdot z \ge 0$ on $\Gamma$.

steps.slogan: Show that the price vector $p$ is strictly positive.
steps.detail: If $p_l = 0$ for some good $l$, then $x_i + e_l$ is affordable and strictly preferred to $x_i$ by strict monotonicity, against the previous step. So $p \gg 0$ and $(p, x)$ is a Walrasian equilibrium.

steps.slogan: Join the two directions into the equivalence.
steps.detail: The budget argument shows that every Walrasian equilibrium allocation lies in the core of every $E_r$. The separation argument shows that every allocation in all the cores is a Walrasian equilibrium allocation. Together they give the equivalence.

concepts.c:preference-relation: Preferences define the strictly preferred net trades and the blocking condition.
concepts.c:walrasian-equilibrium: Prices that make every $x_i$ optimal on its budget set are the target.
concepts.c:core-of-an-economy: Core membership means that no coalition blocks, which both directions use.
concepts.c:convex-set: Convexity of $\Gamma_i$ allows the convex hull and the separation.
concepts.c:hyperplane: The normal of the separating hyperplane becomes the equilibrium price vector.

source.note: The proof of G. Debreu and H. Scarf, A limit theorem on the core of an economy (1963), for equal-treatment allocations.

statement: A positive [even number](c:even-number) $n$ is [perfect](c:perfect-number), that is $\sigma(n) = 2n$ for the [divisor function](c:divisor-function) $\sigma$, if and only if $n = 2^{p-1}(2^p - 1)$ for an integer $p \ge 2$ such that $2^p - 1$ is a [Mersenne prime](c:mersenne-prime).

hypotheses.text: The number $n$ is a positive [even number](c:even-number).

conclusion: $n$ is [perfect](c:perfect-number) if and only if $n = 2^{p-1}(2^p - 1)$ for some $p \ge 2$ with $2^p - 1$ [prime](c:prime-number).

proofs.name: Euclid's form and Euler's converse
proofs.slogan: Euclid's numbers are perfect by multiplicativity, and Euler's argument forces every even perfect number into that form.
proofs.scope: Both directions: Euclid's direction is a computation, and Euler's direction splits $n = 2^k m$ with $m$ odd. The case $p = 1$ is excluded because $2^1 - 1 = 1$ is not prime.

roles.why: An even number is $2^k m$ with $k \ge 1$ and $m$ odd, which splits $\sigma(n)$ into two coprime factors.

steps.slogan: Compute $\sigma$ on powers of two and on products of coprime numbers.
steps.detail: The [divisor function](c:divisor-function) is multiplicative: $\sigma(ab) = \sigma(a)\sigma(b)$ for [coprime](c:coprime-integers) $a, b$. A [geometric series](c:geometric-series) gives $\sigma(2^k) = 1 + 2 + \cdots + 2^k = 2^{k+1} - 1$, and $\sigma(q) = q + 1$ for a prime $q$.

steps.slogan: Show that every number of Euclid's form is perfect.
steps.detail: Let $n = 2^{p-1}q$ with $q = 2^p - 1$ prime. Since $q$ is odd, $2^{p-1}$ and $q$ are coprime, so $\sigma(n) = (2^p - 1)(q + 1) = q \cdot 2^p = 2n$.

steps.slogan: Write an even perfect number as $2^k m$ with $m$ odd and apply $\sigma$.
steps.detail: Let $n = 2^k m$ with $k \ge 1$ and $m$ odd. Multiplicativity gives $\sigma(n) = (2^{k+1} - 1)\sigma(m)$, and perfection says $(2^{k+1} - 1)\sigma(m) = 2^{k+1} m$.

steps.slogan: Show that $2^{k+1} - 1$ divides $m$ and write $m = (2^{k+1} - 1)c$.
steps.detail: The odd number $2^{k+1} - 1$ is coprime to $2^{k+1}$ and divides $2^{k+1} m$, so it divides $m$. Write $m = (2^{k+1} - 1)c$; cancelling $2^{k+1} - 1$ in the equation of the previous step gives $\sigma(m) = 2^{k+1}c$.

steps.slogan: Show that $c = 1$ and that $m$ is prime.
steps.detail: The numbers $1$, $c$ and $m$ divide $m$. If $c > 1$ they are distinct because $c < m$, so $\sigma(m) \ge 1 + c + m = 1 + 2^{k+1}c > \sigma(m)$, a contradiction. So $c = 1$, $m = 2^{k+1} - 1$ and $\sigma(m) = m + 1$, which means that $1$ and $m$ are the only divisors of $m$.

steps.slogan: Read off the form $n = 2^{p-1}(2^p - 1)$ with $p = k + 1$.
steps.detail: With $p = k + 1 \ge 2$ we get $n = 2^{p-1}m = 2^{p-1}(2^p - 1)$, and $2^p - 1 = m$ is a [Mersenne prime](c:mersenne-prime).

steps.slogan: Join the two directions into the equivalence.
steps.detail: Euclid's computation shows that each number $2^{p-1}(2^p - 1)$ with $2^p - 1$ [prime](c:prime-number) is perfect, and Euler's argument shows that each even perfect number has this form. Together they give the equivalence.

concepts.c:even-number: Evenness gives the decomposition $n = 2^k m$ with $m$ odd and $k \ge 1$.
concepts.c:perfect-number: Perfection is the equation $\sigma(n) = 2n$ that the proof solves.
concepts.c:divisor-function: The divisor function $\sigma$ is multiplicative, which splits the equation.
concepts.c:mersenne-prime: The odd factor $2^p - 1$ must be a Mersenne prime.
concepts.c:prime-number: Primality of $2^p - 1$ is the condition in the characterization.
concepts.c:coprime-integers: Coprimality allows $\sigma$ to multiply and lets $2^{k+1} - 1$ divide $m$.

source.note: The classical proof: Euclid (Elements IX.36) for the sufficiency and Euler for the converse.

statement: Let $d \ge 1$. The number $r_d(n)$ of [integer partitions](c:integer-partition) of $n$ into parts not divisible by $d$ equals the number $c_d(n)$ of partitions of $n$ in which no part occurs $d$ or more times, for every $n \ge 0$.

hypotheses.text: The integer $d$ satisfies $d \ge 1$.

proofs.name: Equal generating functions
proofs.slogan: Both counts have the same product as generating function, because the factors $1 - X^{di}$ cancel.
proofs.scope: Every $n \ge 0$ and every $d \ge 1$; the case $d = 1$ gives $0$ for $n > 0$ on both sides. The products are products of formal power series, which converge because the factor for $i$ differs from $1$ only in degrees $\ge i$.

roles.why: The bound $d \ge 1$ makes the multiplicities $0, \dots, d-1$ a nonempty range and the geometric sum valid.

steps.slogan: Write the [generating function](c:generating-function) of $r_d(n)$ as a product over the allowed parts.
steps.detail: A partition into parts not divisible by $d$ chooses a multiplicity $j \ge 0$ for each allowed part $i$. Expanding the product gives $\sum_n r_d(n)X^n = \prod_{d \nmid i} \sum_{j \ge 0} X^{ij} = \prod_{d \nmid i}(1 - X^i)^{-1}$ in the ring of [formal power series](c:formal-power-series), by the [geometric series](c:geometric-series).

steps.slogan: Write the generating function of $c_d(n)$ as a product over all parts.
steps.detail: Here part $i$ may occur $0, 1, \dots, d-1$ times, so $\sum_n c_d(n)X^n = \prod_{i \ge 1}(1 + X^i + \cdots + X^{(d-1)i}) = \prod_{i \ge 1} \frac{1 - X^{di}}{1 - X^i}$, using $(1 + t + \cdots + t^{d-1})(1 - t) = 1 - t^d$.

steps.slogan: Cancel the common factors to show that the two products are equal.
steps.detail: Every index $i \ge 1$ is either not divisible by $d$ or equals $di'$, so $\prod_{i \ge 1}(1 - X^i) = \prod_{d \nmid i}(1 - X^i) \cdot \prod_{i \ge 1}(1 - X^{di})$. Dividing by the nonzero series $\prod_{i \ge 1}(1 - X^i)$ gives $\prod_{d \nmid i}(1 - X^i)^{-1} = \prod_{i \ge 1}(1 - X^{di})/(1 - X^i)$.

steps.slogan: Compare the coefficients of $X^n$ in the two equal series.
steps.detail: Equal power series have equal coefficients, so $r_d(n) = c_d(n)$ for every $n \ge 0$.

concepts.c:integer-partition: The two counts are numbers of partitions with different restrictions.
concepts.c:generating-function: Generating functions turn the counting problem into an identity of series.
concepts.c:formal-power-series: The products live in the ring of formal power series, where coefficients compare.
concepts.c:geometric-series: Geometric series give each factor and the cancellation $(1 + t + \cdots)(1 - t)$.

statement: In every [group](c:group), with the [commutator](c:commutator) $[x,y] = xyx^{-1}y^{-1}$, all elements $a, b, c$ satisfy $[[a,b],\, bcb^{-1}]\,[[b,c],\, cac^{-1}]\,[[c,a],\, aba^{-1}] = 1$, where $bcb^{-1}$, $cac^{-1}$ and $aba^{-1}$ are [conjugates](c:conjugation).

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a [group](c:group) and $a, b, c \in G$.

conclusion: The product $[[a,b],\, bcb^{-1}]\,[[b,c],\, cac^{-1}]\,[[c,a],\, aba^{-1}]$ equals the identity $1$.

formal.difference: The declaration is the additive-notation twin of commutatorElement_commutatorElement_conj_mul, which states this identity multiplicatively with the same commutator convention.

proofs.name: Expansion and cancellation
proofs.slogan: Expand the three factors as words in $a, b, c$ and cancel adjacent inverse pairs until the empty word remains.
proofs.scope: Every group, with no assumption such as commutativity or finiteness. The proof is a computation in the free group on $a, b, c$, which maps onto every group generated by three elements.

roles.why: In a group, products are associative and every letter has an inverse, so adjacent inverse pairs cancel.

steps.slogan: Expand the first factor into a word in $a, b, c$ and cancel.
steps.detail: With $[x,y] = xyx^{-1}y^{-1}$, the first factor is $(aba^{-1}b^{-1})(bcb^{-1})(bab^{-1}a^{-1})(bc^{-1}b^{-1})$. Cancelling the adjacent pairs $b^{-1}b$ leaves the word $T(a,b,c) = aba^{-1}\,c\,ab^{-1}a^{-1}\,bc^{-1}b^{-1}$.

steps.slogan: Rotate the letters cyclically to get the other two factors.
steps.detail: The second and third factors arise from the first by the substitution $a \to b \to c \to a$ and its square. So they equal $T(b,c,a) = bcb^{-1}\,a\,bc^{-1}b^{-1}\,ca^{-1}c^{-1}$ and $T(c,a,b) = cac^{-1}\,b\,ca^{-1}c^{-1}\,ab^{-1}a^{-1}$.

steps.slogan: Cancel the two junctions between consecutive words.
steps.detail: The tail $bc^{-1}b^{-1}$ of $T(a,b,c)$ is the inverse of the head $bcb^{-1}$ of $T(b,c,a)$, so both vanish. In the same way the tail $ca^{-1}c^{-1}$ of $T(b,c,a)$ cancels the head $cac^{-1}$ of $T(c,a,b)$.

steps.slogan: Reduce the remaining word to the empty word.
steps.detail: What remains is $aba^{-1}cab^{-1}a^{-1} \cdot abc^{-1}b^{-1} \cdot bca^{-1}c^{-1}ab^{-1}a^{-1}$. Cancelling $a^{-1}a$, $b^{-1}b$, $b^{-1}b$, $c^{-1}c$, $aa^{-1}$, $cc^{-1}$, $a^{-1}a$, $bb^{-1}$ and $aa^{-1}$ in this order leaves the empty word, which is $1$.

concepts.c:group: Group axioms justify cancelling adjacent inverse pairs in a product.
concepts.c:commutator: The identity is a relation among iterated commutators, which the proof expands.
concepts.c:conjugation: The second entries of the outer commutators are conjugates, expanded as $bcb^{-1}$.

statement: Let $H = p^2/2m + \varphi(x;V)$ be the [Hamiltonian](c:hamiltonian) of a one-dimensional system with a U-shaped potential $\varphi$. For an energy $E$, let $\langle\cdot\rangle_t$ be the [time average](c:time-average) over one period, and put $T = 2\langle K\rangle_t$ with $K = p^2/2m$, $P = \langle -\partial_V\varphi\rangle_t$ and $S = \log\oint p\,dx$. Then $dS = (dE + P\,dV)/T$.

hypotheses.text: The [Hamiltonian](c:hamiltonian) is $H = p^2/2m + \varphi(x;V)$ with $m > 0$, and $\varphi$ is smooth in $x$ and $V$.
For each energy $E$ above the minimum of $\varphi$, the set $\{\varphi < E\}$ is a bounded interval $(x_-, x_+)$ with $\varphi'(x_\pm) \ne 0$.

conclusion: $\partial S/\partial E = 1/T$ and $\partial S/\partial V = P/T$, so $dS = (dE + P\,dV)/T$.

proofs.name: Action integral and period
proofs.slogan: Write the action as an integral over the orbit, then differentiate it in $E$ and $V$ to get the period and the pressure.
proofs.scope: Energies above the minimum of $\varphi$, where the orbit is a periodic motion between simple turning points. Differentiation under the integral sign is justified because the integrand vanishes at the turning points and the $E$-derivative has an integrable inverse square-root singularity.

roles.why: The form $p^2/2m + \varphi$ gives $p = \pm\sqrt{2m(E - \varphi)}$ and $dt = m\,dx/p$.
A U-shaped potential makes every orbit periodic between simple turning points, so the action and its derivatives exist.

steps.slogan: Write the action $I(E,V) = \oint p\,dx$ as an integral over the orbit.
steps.detail: On the orbit $p = \pm\sqrt{2m(E - \varphi)}$, so $I(E,V) = 2\int_{x_-}^{x_+}\sqrt{2m(E - \varphi(x;V))}\,dx$, the phase-space area enclosed by the orbit and an [adiabatic invariant](c:adiabatic-invariant). Hamilton's equation $\dot x = p/m$ gives $dt = m\,dx/p$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\partial_E I$ equals the period $\tau$.
steps.detail: Differentiating under the integral sign gives $\partial_E\sqrt{2m(E - \varphi)} = m/p$. The endpoint terms vanish because the integrand is $0$ at the turning points, and the singularity of $m/p$ there is integrable since $\varphi'(x_\pm) \ne 0$. So $\partial_E I = \oint m\,dx/p = \oint dt = \tau$.

steps.slogan: Express the [time average](c:time-average) of the kinetic energy through $I$.
steps.detail: Since $K\,dt = (p^2/2m)(m\,dx/p) = \tfrac12 p\,dx$, we get $\int_0^\tau K\,dt = \tfrac12 I$. So $\langle K\rangle_t = I/(2\tau)$ and $T = 2\langle K\rangle_t = I/\tau$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\partial_V I$ equals $\tau P$.
steps.detail: The [partial derivative](c:partial-derivative) of the integrand is $\partial_V\sqrt{2m(E - \varphi)} = -m\,\partial_V\varphi/p$. Hence $\partial_V I = -\oint \partial_V\varphi\,dt = \tau\,\langle -\partial_V\varphi\rangle_t = \tau P$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate $S = \log I$ and compare with $T$ and $P$.
steps.detail: By the period step and the kinetic step, $\partial_E S = \partial_E I/I = \tau/I = 1/T$. By the pressure step, $\partial_V S = \partial_V I/I = \tau P/I = P/T$. Hence $dS = \partial_E S\,dE + \partial_V S\,dV = (dE + P\,dV)/T$.

concepts.c:hamiltonian: The Hamiltonian gives the momentum on the orbit and the equations of motion.
concepts.c:time-average: The temperature $T$ and the pressure $P$ are time averages over one period.
concepts.c:adiabatic-invariant: The action $I$ is the adiabatic invariant whose logarithm is the entropy.
concepts.c:partial-derivative: The pressure comes from the partial derivative of $\varphi$ in the parameter $V$.

source.note: A direct derivation from the action integral and the period, written out here; the statement follows the Wikipedia article on the Helmholtz theorem (classical mechanics).

statement: Let $p$ be an odd prime, let $A$ be the $p$-part of the [ideal class group](c:ideal-class-group) of the [cyclotomic field](c:cyclotomic-field) $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$, and let $A_i$ be its $\omega^i$-eigenspace for $\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)/\mathbb{Q})$, where $\omega$ is the Teichmüller character. For odd $i$ with $3 \le i \le p - 2$, $A_i \ne 0$ if and only if $p$ divides the numerator of the [Bernoulli number](c:bernoulli-number) $B_{p-i}$.

hypotheses.text: The number $p$ is an odd prime.
The index $i$ is odd with $3 \le i \le p - 2$.

conclusion: $A_i \ne 0$ if and only if $p$ divides the numerator of $B_{p-i}$.

proofs.name: Stickelberger and Ribet's modular construction
proofs.slogan: Stickelberger's relation gives one direction, and a cusp form congruent to an Eisenstein series gives an unramified extension for the other.
proofs.scope: The eigenspaces $A_i$ with odd $i$ in the stated range; Herbrand proved that $A_i \ne 0$ implies $p \mid B_{p-i}$ and Ribet proved the converse. The steps outline the cited papers and rest on them for the modular and Galois-theoretic details.

roles.why: An odd prime gives a field whose Galois group has order prime to $p$, so $A$ splits into eigenspaces.
Odd $i$ in this range makes $B_{p-i}$ an even-index, $p$-integral Bernoulli number and avoids the exceptional eigenspace $A_1$.

steps.slogan: Use Stickelberger's relation to show that $A_i \ne 0$ forces $p \mid B_{p-i}$.
steps.detail: This is Herbrand's direction. The Stickelberger element annihilates the class group, and its $\omega^i$-component acts on $A_i$ as multiplication by a $p$-adic number congruent to $B_{p-i}/(p-i)$ modulo $p$. If $A_i \ne 0$, this number is not a unit, so $p \mid B_{p-i}$.

steps.slogan: Ribet's direction: build a cusp form congruent to an Eisenstein series modulo $p$.
steps.detail: If $p \mid B_{p-i}$, the constant term of a weight-two [Eisenstein series](c:eisenstein-series) of level $p$, attached to a power of $\omega$, is divisible by a prime above $p$. Ribet shows that this gives a normalized [cusp form](c:cusp-form) of level $p$, a [modular form](c:modular-form) whose Hecke eigenvalues are congruent to those of the Eisenstein series.

steps.slogan: Attach a Galois representation to the cusp form and see that its reduction is reducible.
steps.detail: Deligne's theorem attaches a two-dimensional $p$-adic [Galois representation](c:galois-representation) to the eigenform. By the eigenvalue congruence and the Chebotarev density theorem, its reduction modulo a prime above $p$ has as semisimplification a sum of two characters that are powers of $\omega$.

steps.slogan: Choose a stable lattice whose reduction is a nonsplit extension of the two characters.
steps.detail: The representation itself is irreducible because the form is cuspidal. Ribet's lattice argument then gives a stable lattice whose reduction is a nonsplit extension of one character by the other, in the order that the proof needs.

steps.slogan: Cut out an unramified extension of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$ and apply class field theory.
steps.detail: The nonsplit extension gives a cohomology class, hence a degree-$p$ Galois extension of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$ on which $\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)/\mathbb{Q})$ acts through $\omega^i$. It is unramified away from $p$ because the level is $p$, and unramified at $p$ by a local analysis of the representation. Inside the [Hilbert class field](c:hilbert-class-field) it gives a quotient of $A$ with action $\omega^i$, so $A_i \ne 0$.

steps.slogan: Join Herbrand's direction and Ribet's direction into the equivalence.
steps.detail: Herbrand's step shows that $A_i \ne 0$ implies $p \mid B_{p-i}$, and Ribet's construction shows that $p \mid B_{p-i}$ implies $A_i \ne 0$. Together they give the equivalence for odd $i$ with $3 \le i \le p-2$.

concepts.c:ideal-class-group: The class group is the object whose eigenspaces $A_i$ the theorem describes.
concepts.c:cyclotomic-field: The field $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$ carries the Galois action that splits $A$.
concepts.c:bernoulli-number: The divisibility of $B_{p-i}$ by $p$ is the numerical criterion.
concepts.c:eisenstein-series: The Eisenstein series has constant term divisible by $p$ exactly when $p \mid B_{p-i}$.
concepts.c:cusp-form: The congruent cusp form supplies an irreducible Galois representation.
concepts.c:modular-form: Modular forms of level $p$ carry the Hecke eigenvalues that are compared modulo $p$.
concepts.c:galois-representation: Its reduction yields the nonsplit extension that becomes an unramified field extension.
concepts.c:hilbert-class-field: The unramified extension lies in the Hilbert class field, which class field theory ties to $A$.

source.ref: K. A. Ribet, A modular construction of unramified p-extensions of Q(mu_p), Inventiones Mathematicae 34 (1976), 151-162
source.note: Ribet's paper gives steps 2 to 5; Herbrand's direction (J. Herbrand, Sur les classes des corps circulaires, Journal de Mathematiques Pures et Appliquees 11 (1932), 417-441) is step 1.

statement: For every [real number](c:real-number) $x$ and every integer $n \ge 1$, $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \lfloor x + k/n \rfloor = \lfloor nx \rfloor$, where $\lfloor\cdot\rfloor$ is the [floor function](c:floor-function).

hypotheses.text: The number $x$ is a [real number](c:real-number).
The number $n$ is an integer with $n \ge 1$.

formal.difference: The declaration holds in any linearly ordered field with a floor function, and it also covers $n = 0$, where both sides are $0$.

proofs.name: Reduction to integer division
proofs.slogan: Replace each term by an integer quotient of $\lfloor nx \rfloor + k$ by $n$, then count how often the quotient jumps.
proofs.scope: Every real $x$ and every integer $n \ge 1$. The case $n = 0$ is trivial because both sides are $0$.

roles.why: The [floor function](c:floor-function) of $nx$ is defined for a real $x$ and gives the integer $a$ that replaces $nx$.
A positive $n$ allows division with remainder and makes the sum consist of exactly $n$ terms.

steps.slogan: Replace $\lfloor x + k/n \rfloor$ by $\lfloor (\lfloor nx \rfloor + k)/n \rfloor$.
steps.detail: We have $x + k/n = (nx + k)/n$. For a real $z$ and a positive integer $n$, $\lfloor z/n \rfloor = \lfloor \lfloor z \rfloor/n \rfloor$, because for an integer $q$ we have $q \le z/n \iff qn \le z \iff qn \le \lfloor z \rfloor$. Also $\lfloor nx + k \rfloor = \lfloor nx \rfloor + k$ for an integer $k$.

steps.slogan: Write $a = \lfloor nx \rfloor$ as $qn + r$ with $0 \le r < n$.
steps.detail: By division with remainder there are integers $q$ and $r$ with $a = qn + r$ and $0 \le r < n$. Here $a$ is the integer from the previous step.

steps.slogan: Show that the $k$-th term is $q$ for $k < n - r$ and $q + 1$ otherwise.
steps.detail: For $0 \le k < n$ we have $a + k = qn + (r + k)$ with $0 \le r + k < 2n$. So the integer part of $(a + k)/n$ is $q + \lfloor (r + k)/n \rfloor$, which is $q$ if $r + k < n$ and $q + 1$ if $r + k \ge n$.

steps.slogan: Add the $n$ terms and count the indices $k$ with $k \ge n - r$.
steps.detail: Exactly $r$ indices $k \in \{n - r, \dots, n - 1\}$ give $q + 1$, and the other $n - r$ indices give $q$. The sum is $nq + r = a = \lfloor nx \rfloor$.

concepts.c:real-number: The identity holds for every real $x$, through the integer $\lfloor nx \rfloor$.
concepts.c:floor-function: The floor function on both sides turns the identity into integer arithmetic.

source.note: mathlib rewrites each term as (floor (n x) + k) / n in integer division with floor_add_natCast and floor_div_natCast, then sums with Int.sum_range_add_ediv.

statement: Let $f$ be a real function [differentiable](c:differentiable-function) at a real number $x$, extended to the hyperreals by transfer, and let $\Delta x$ be an [infinitesimal](c:infinitesimal). Then $\Delta y = f(x + \Delta x) - f(x) = f'(x)\,\Delta x + \varepsilon\,\Delta x$ for some infinitesimal $\varepsilon$. If $\Delta x \ne 0$, then $\Delta y/\Delta x$ is infinitely close to the [derivative](c:derivative) $f'(x)$.

hypotheses.text: The real function $f$ is [differentiable](c:differentiable-function) at the real number $x$, and $f$ is extended to the hyperreal numbers by transfer.
The hyperreal number $\Delta x$ is [infinitesimal](c:infinitesimal): $|\Delta x| < \delta$ for every real $\delta > 0$.

conclusion: There is an infinitesimal $\varepsilon$ with $\Delta y = f'(x)\,\Delta x + \varepsilon\,\Delta x$, and for $\Delta x \ne 0$ the quotient $\Delta y/\Delta x$ is infinitely close to $f'(x)$.

proofs.name: Transfer of the epsilon-delta sentence
proofs.slogan: Transfer the epsilon-delta form of differentiability to the hyperreals, then define $\varepsilon$ as the error of the difference quotient.
proofs.scope: All infinitesimal $\Delta x$, including $\Delta x = 0$, where both sides vanish for any $\varepsilon$. The function is the natural extension of a real function, and the transfer principle applies to first-order sentences with real parameters.

roles.why: Differentiability gives, for each real $\delta$, a real $\eta$ that bounds the error of the difference quotient.
An infinitesimal $\Delta x$ is smaller than every real $\eta > 0$, so the transferred bound applies to it.

steps.slogan: State differentiability as a first-order sentence with real $\delta$ and $\eta$.
steps.detail: Differentiability at $x$ says: for every real $\delta > 0$ there is a real $\eta > 0$ such that for all real $h$ with $0 < |h| < \eta$, $|(f(x + h) - f(x))/h - f'(x)| < \delta$.

steps.slogan: Transfer this sentence to the hyperreal numbers.
steps.detail: Fix a real $\delta > 0$ and its real $\eta$. The statement about all real $h$ with $0 < |h| < \eta$ has real parameters $f$, $x$, $f'(x)$, $\delta$ and $\eta$. By the transfer principle it holds for all hyperreal $h$ with $0 < |h| < \eta$, with $f$ replaced by its extension.

steps.slogan: Define $\varepsilon$ as the error of the difference quotient.
steps.detail: Put $\varepsilon = \Delta y/\Delta x - f'(x)$ if $\Delta x \ne 0$, and $\varepsilon = 0$ if $\Delta x = 0$. In both cases $\Delta y = f'(x)\,\Delta x + \varepsilon\,\Delta x$, because for $\Delta x = 0$ both sides are $0$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\varepsilon$ is smaller than every positive real number.
steps.detail: Fix a real $\delta > 0$ with its real $\eta$. If $\Delta x \ne 0$, then $0 < |\Delta x| < \eta$ because $\Delta x$ is infinitesimal, so the transferred sentence gives $|\varepsilon| < \delta$. If $\Delta x = 0$, then $\varepsilon = 0 < \delta$. Hence $\varepsilon$ is infinitesimal.

steps.slogan: Divide by $\Delta x \ne 0$ to compare the quotient with $f'(x)$.
steps.detail: For $\Delta x \ne 0$ we get $\Delta y/\Delta x = f'(x) + \varepsilon$ with infinitesimal $\varepsilon$. So the quotient is infinitely close to the [derivative](c:derivative) $f'(x)$, which is its standard part.

concepts.c:differentiable-function: Differentiability supplies the epsilon-delta sentence that is transferred.
concepts.c:infinitesimal: Infinitesimal increments are smaller than the real $\eta$ of the transferred sentence.
concepts.c:derivative: The derivative is the standard part of the difference quotient.

source.note: The standard transfer proof of the increment theorem, as in Keisler, Elementary Calculus: An Infinitesimal Approach, chapter 2.

statement: Let $f : A \to B$ be a map between types of a univalent universe $U$. Form the join powers $f^{*1} = f$ and $f^{*(n+1)} = f^{*n} * f$, using the [join of maps](c:join-of-maps) over $B$, with domains $A_n$ and maps $A_n \to A_{n+1}$. The [sequential colimit](c:sequential-colimit) $A_\infty$ gives a factorization $A \to A_\infty \to B$ that is the [image factorization](c:image-factorization) of $f$, and $A_\infty$ lies in $U$.

hypotheses.text: The map $f : A \to B$ is a map between types of a univalent universe $U$ that is closed under [pushouts](c:pushout) and sequential colimits.

conclusion: The factorization $A \to A_\infty \to B$ is the [image factorization](c:image-factorization): the first map is a [surjection](c:surjection), the second is an [embedding](c:embedding), and $A_\infty$ lies in $U$.

proofs.name: Join powers and a propositional colimit
proofs.slogan: The fibres of the colimit of join powers are propositions, and induction on the stage shows that the map from $A$ is surjective.
proofs.scope: The theorem for an arbitrary map $f$ in a univalent universe closed under pushouts and sequential colimits. The steps outline the cited paper and rest on it for the proposition step.

roles.why: The universe supplies pushouts, sequential colimits and univalence, so the join powers and their colimit exist and stay in $U$.

steps.slogan: Form the join powers of $f$ as iterated fibrewise joins over $B$.
steps.detail: The [join of maps](c:join-of-maps) $f * g$ over $B$ is the [pushout](c:pushout) of $A \leftarrow A \times_B A' \to A'$ with its map to $B$, and its fibre over $b$ is the join of the two fibres. Put $A_1 = A$ and $A_{n+1} = A_n *_B A$. The fibre of $A_n$ over $b$ is then the $n$-fold join $F_b^{*n}$ of $F_b = \mathrm{fib}_f(b)$.

steps.slogan: Take the sequential colimit of the inclusions $A_n \to A_{n+1}$ over $B$.
steps.detail: The inclusions $A_n \to A_n *_B A$ form a sequence over $B$. Its [sequential colimit](c:sequential-colimit) $A_\infty$ comes with maps $A \to A_\infty \to B$. Colimits are stable under pullback, so the fibre of $A_\infty$ over $b$ is the colimit $F_b^{*\infty}$ of the join powers $F_b^{*n}$.

steps.slogan: Show that the colimit of the join powers of any type is a proposition.
steps.detail: For every type $F$, the colimit $F^{*\infty}$ of its join powers is a [mere proposition](c:mere-proposition); this is van Doorn's construction of the propositional truncation, which the paper generalizes from types to maps. Applied to $F = F_b$, every fibre of $A_\infty \to B$ is a proposition.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the map $A_\infty \to B$ is an embedding.
steps.detail: A map whose fibres are propositions is an [embedding](c:embedding). By the two previous steps, every fibre of $A_\infty \to B$ is a proposition.

steps.slogan: Show that $A \to A_\infty$ is a surjection by induction on the stage.
steps.detail: A point of the fibre $F_b^{*\infty}$ lies in some $F_b^{*n}$. By induction on $n$, each $F_b^{*n}$ gives $\|F_b\|$: the case $n = 1$ is clear, and a join of two types that give $\|F_b\|$ gives it too, since $\|F_b\|$ is a proposition. As the fibre is a proposition, $F_b \to F_b^{*\infty}$ is a [surjection](c:surjection), and so is $A \to A_\infty$.

steps.slogan: Check that every $A_n$ and the colimit $A_\infty$ lie in $U$.
steps.detail: The universe $U$ is closed under pullbacks, pushouts and sequential colimits, so each $A_n$ and $A_\infty$ lie in $U$. No propositional truncation is used, which is the point of the construction.

steps.slogan: Identify the factorization as the image factorization of $f$.
steps.detail: A factorization of $f$ into a surjection followed by an embedding is unique up to equivalence. So $A \to A_\infty \to B$ is the [image factorization](c:image-factorization), with the image $A_\infty$ in $U$.

concepts.c:join-of-maps: The join of maps over $B$ builds the join powers of $f$.
concepts.c:sequential-colimit: The sequential colimit of the join powers is the image.
concepts.c:image-factorization: The construction produces the image factorization of $f$.
concepts.c:pushout: Pushouts define the join of maps and keep the construction in $U$.
concepts.c:surjection: Surjectivity of $A \to A_\infty$ is half of the image factorization.
concepts.c:embedding: Embedding of $A_\infty \to B$ is the other half of the factorization.
concepts.c:mere-proposition: Propositional fibres make the colimit map an embedding.

source.ref: E. Rijke, The join construction, arXiv:1701.07538 (2017)
source.note: Rijke defines the join of maps and constructs the image as the colimit of the join powers; the proposition step builds on van Doorn's construction of the propositional truncation.

statement: Let $S = 1 + iT$ be the unitary [S-matrix](c:s-matrix) of a perturbative theory regulated by a mass $\lambda > 0$, and let $S$ conserve energy. Let $D$ be the set of all states with energy in a fixed window. Then, order by order in the coupling, $\sum_{f \in D}|S_{fi}|^2 = 1$ for every $i \in D$: the divergent virtual and real-emission terms cancel for every $\lambda$, so the limit $\lambda \to 0$ is finite.

hypotheses.text: The [S-matrix](c:s-matrix) $S = 1 + iT$ of the regulated theory is unitary.
The matrix $S$ conserves energy: it commutes with the [Hamiltonian](c:hamiltonian).
The set $D$ consists of all states with energy in a fixed window whose width does not depend on $\lambda$.
The amplitudes are expanded in powers of the coupling $g$ at fixed $\lambda$.

conclusion: For every $i \in D$, the sum $\sum_{f \in D}|S_{fi}|^2$ equals $1$ at order $g^0$ and $0$ at every higher order, for every $\lambda > 0$, so it has a finite limit as $\lambda \to 0$.

proofs.name: Unitarity inside the degenerate set
proofs.slogan: Sum over the whole degenerate set, where unitarity makes the total probability exactly one, so the divergences must cancel.
proofs.scope: The Lee-Nauenberg form of the KLN theorem for one regulated theory, with formal perturbative sums over states. Kinoshita's diagram-level analysis of mass singularities and the application to the Standard Model are not outlined here.

roles.why: Unitarity gives $S^\dagger S = 1$, the identity that makes the summed probability equal one.
Energy conservation makes $S$ preserve the energy window, so $D$ is closed under $S$.
A window of fixed width keeps the same set $D$ of states that become degenerate as $\lambda \to 0$.
The identity holds as a power series in $g$, so it splits into one identity per order.

steps.slogan: Collect all states with energy in the window into the degenerate set $D$.
steps.detail: Fix a window $[E - \delta, E + \delta]$ whose width does not depend on $\lambda$. The states that become degenerate as $\lambda \to 0$, such as those with soft or collinear emission, lie in this window for all small $\lambda$, so $D$ is the same set for every $\lambda$.

steps.slogan: Show that $S$ maps $D$ into itself.
steps.detail: Energy conservation means that $S$ commutes with the [Hamiltonian](c:hamiltonian), so it preserves each energy value. A superposition of states with energies in the window is sent to such a superposition, so $S$ and $S^\dagger$ both map $D$ into $D$ and $S$ restricts to a unitary operator on $D$.

steps.slogan: Restrict unitarity to $D$ and expand in the coupling.
steps.detail: On $D$, [unitarity](c:unitary-operator) gives $\sum_{f \in D}|S_{fi}|^2 = 1$ for each $i \in D$, equivalently $-i(T - T^\dagger) = T^\dagger T$. Expand $T = \sum_n g^n T_n$; at order $g^n$ the right side sums over intermediate states in $D$ because $T$ maps $D$ into $D$.

steps.slogan: Match the divergent virtual terms with the divergent real-emission terms.
steps.detail: As $\lambda \to 0$, the terms of $T - T^\dagger$ (loop [Feynman diagrams](c:feynman-diagram)) and the terms of $T^\dagger T$ (phase-space integrals over states of $D$) diverge separately. The order-by-order identity shows that the divergences cancel exactly in $\sum_{f \in D}|S_{fi}|^2$, for every $\lambda$.

steps.slogan: Read off the limit $\lambda \to 0$ of the sum.
steps.detail: The sum is $1$ at order $g^0$ and $0$ at every order $g^n$ with $n \ge 1$, whatever $\lambda$ is. So the limit $\lambda \to 0$ exists and is finite, and an average over initial states $i \in D$ with fixed weights has the same limit.

concepts.c:s-matrix: The S-matrix holds the transition amplitudes whose squares are the probabilities.
concepts.c:hamiltonian: Commuting with the Hamiltonian is energy conservation, which keeps states in the window.
concepts.c:unitary-operator: Unitarity makes the total probability over the closed set $D$ equal to one.
concepts.c:feynman-diagram: Loop diagrams and real-emission diagrams carry the divergences that cancel.

source.ref: T. D. Lee and M. Nauenberg, Degenerate systems and mass singularities, Physical Review 133 (1964), B1549-B1562
source.note: Lee and Nauenberg prove the cancellation by unitarity within the degenerate set; T. Kinoshita, Mass singularities of Feynman amplitudes, Journal of Mathematical Physics 3 (1962), 650-677, gave the earlier diagram-level analysis.

statement: Let $f(1) \le f(2) \le \cdots$ be a [monotone sequence](c:monotone-sequence) of nonnegative integers, and let $f^*(n) = \#\{m \ge 1 : f(m) < n\}$. The sequences $F(m) = f(m) + m$ and $G(n) = f^*(n) + n$, with infinite terms of $G$ dropped, are [complementary sequences](c:complementary-sequences): every positive integer is a term of exactly one of them, and occurs there once.

hypotheses.text: The sequence $f$ is a [nondecreasing](c:monotone-sequence) sequence of nonnegative integers.

conclusion: Every positive integer occurs exactly once among the terms of $F$ and $G$ taken together.

proofs.name: Threshold counting
proofs.slogan: Monotonicity makes $f(m) < n$ equivalent to $m \le f^*(n)$, and this equivalence separates and covers the integers.
proofs.scope: All nondecreasing $f$, including bounded $f$ where $f^*(n)$ can be infinite and those terms of $G$ are dropped. The converse, that every complementary pair arises from some $f$, is not proved here.

roles.why: Monotonicity makes $\{m : f(m) < n\}$ an initial segment and keeps $F$ and $G$ increasing.

steps.slogan: Show that $f(m) < n$ holds exactly when $m \le f^*(n)$.
steps.detail: Because $f$ is nondecreasing, $\{m : f(m) < n\}$ is an initial segment $\{1, \dots, f^*(n)\}$ of the positive integers. So $f(m) < n$ if and only if $m \le f^*(n)$.

steps.slogan: Show that $F$ and $G$ are strictly increasing.
steps.detail: We have $F(m+1) - F(m) = f(m+1) - f(m) + 1 \ge 1$. The sets $\{m : f(m) < n\}$ grow with $n$, so $f^*$ is nondecreasing and $G(n+1) - G(n) \ge 1$. So each positive integer occurs at most once in each sequence.

steps.slogan: Show that no term of $F$ equals a term of $G$.
steps.detail: If $f(m) < n$, the threshold step gives $m \le f^*(n)$, so $F(m) < n + f^*(n) = G(n)$. If $f(m) \ge n$, it gives $m \ge f^*(n) + 1$, so $F(m) \ge n + f^*(n) + 1 > G(n)$.

steps.slogan: Show that every positive integer $N$ outside $F$ is a term of $G$.
steps.detail: Let $a = \#\{m : F(m) \le N\}$, finite because $F(m) \ge m$, and put $n = N - a$. If $N$ is not a value of $F$, then $F(a) < N < F(a+1)$ (with $N < F(1)$ if $a = 0$), so $n \ge 1$, $f(a) < n$ and $f(a+1) \ge n$. By monotonicity $f^*(n) = a$, so $G(n) = a + n = N$.

steps.slogan: Combine the three counts into the partition of the positive integers.
steps.detail: The increasing step gives at most one occurrence in each sequence, the disjointness step gives no occurrence in both, and the covering step gives at least one occurrence. So each positive integer occurs exactly once among the terms of $F$ and $G$.

concepts.c:monotone-sequence: Monotonicity of $f$ gives the initial segments that define the inverse $f^*$.
concepts.c:complementary-sequences: The theorem says that $F$ and $G$ split the positive integers.

source.note: A direct counting proof; the theorem is from J. Lambek and L. Moser, Inverse and complementary sequences of natural numbers, American Mathematical Monthly 61 (1954), 454-458.

statement: Consider the [ordinary differential equation](c:ordinary-differential-equation) $\dot x = Ax + X(x,y)$, $\dot y = Y(x,y)$ with $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$, where every [eigenvalue](c:eigenvalue) of $A$ has negative real part, the maps $X, Y$ are [continuously differentiable](c:continuously-differentiable-map) near $0$, $X(0,y) = Y(0,y) = 0$ and $\partial_x X(0,0) = 0$. Then the origin is [Lyapunov stable](c:lyapunov-stability), and nearby solutions have $x(t) \to 0$ exponentially and $y(t) \to y_\infty$, a point near $y(0)$.

hypotheses.text: Every [eigenvalue](c:eigenvalue) of the $n \times n$ matrix $A$ has negative real part.
The maps $X, Y$ are [continuously differentiable](c:continuously-differentiable-map) near $0$ and $X(0,y) = Y(0,y) = 0$, so every point $(0,y)$ is an equilibrium.
The derivative of $X$ in $x$ vanishes at the origin: $\partial_x X(0,0) = 0$.

conclusion: The origin is [Lyapunov stable](c:lyapunov-stability), and there are constants $C, \alpha > 0$ and $\delta > 0$ such that every solution with $|x_0| + |y_0| < \delta$ exists for all $t \ge 0$, with $|x(t)| \le C|x_0|e^{-\alpha t}$ and $y(t) \to y_\infty$ for some $y_\infty$ with $|y_\infty - y_0| \le C|x_0|$.

proofs.name: Variation of constants and a bootstrap
proofs.slogan: Bound $x$ by variation of constants and Gronwall, bound the drift of $y$ by the integral of $x$, and close the estimates by continuity.
proofs.scope: Solutions that start in a small ball; the constants $C$, $\alpha$ and $\delta$ depend only on the system. The norm is $|x| + |y|$, and local existence and uniqueness follow from the $C^1$ hypothesis.

roles.why: Negative real parts make $e^{At}$ decay exponentially, which makes $x$ decay.
Vanishing on $x = 0$ bounds $Y$ by $L|x|$, so the drift of $y$ is controlled by the decaying $x$.
A zero derivative of $X$ in $x$ makes the coupling constant $\kappa$ small near the origin, which the Gronwall step needs.

steps.slogan: Bound the matrix exponential and the nonlinear terms near the origin.
steps.detail: Since $A$ has eigenvalues with negative real parts, $\|e^{At}\| \le Ke^{-2\alpha t}$ for some $K \ge 1$ and $\alpha > 0$. Fix $\kappa$ with $K\kappa \le \alpha$. As $X, Y$ are $C^1$ with $X(0,y) = Y(0,y) = 0$ and $\partial_x X(0,0) = 0$, there are $r > 0$ and $L$ with $|X(x,y)| \le \kappa|x|$ and $|Y(x,y)| \le L|x|$ whenever $|x| + |y| < r$.

steps.slogan: Show that $x$ decays exponentially while the solution stays in the ball.
steps.detail: Suppose $|x(s)| + |y(s)| < r$ for $0 \le s \le t$. Variation of constants gives $|x(t)| \le Ke^{-2\alpha t}|x_0| + \int_0^t K\kappa\,e^{-2\alpha(t-s)}|x(s)|\,ds$. Gronwall's lemma applied to $e^{2\alpha t}|x(t)|$ gives $|x(t)| \le K|x_0|e^{-(2\alpha - K\kappa)t} \le K|x_0|e^{-\alpha t}$.

steps.slogan: Bound the drift of $y$ by the integral of $|x|$.
steps.detail: While the solution stays in the ball, $|y(t) - y_0| \le \int_0^t L|x(s)|\,ds \le LK|x_0|/\alpha$. Hence $|x(t)| + |y(t)| \le C(|x_0| + |y_0|)$ with $C = 1 + K + LK/\alpha$.

steps.slogan: Show that a solution that starts small never leaves the ball.
steps.detail: Let $|x_0| + |y_0| < \delta = r/(2C)$. If the solution reached the sphere of radius $r$, take the first such time $t^*$; the estimates on $[0, t^*]$ give $|x(t^*)| + |y(t^*)| \le C\delta = r/2$, a contradiction. So the solution stays in the ball and, being bounded, exists for all $t \ge 0$.

steps.slogan: Show that $y(t)$ converges and $x(t)$ tends to zero.
steps.detail: For all $t$, $|x(t)| \le K|x_0|e^{-\alpha t} \to 0$. The integral $\int_0^\infty |Y(x,y)|\,ds \le LK|x_0|/\alpha$ is finite, so $y(t) = y_0 + \int_0^t Y\,ds$ converges to some $y_\infty$ with $|y_\infty - y_0| \le LK|x_0|/\alpha$.

steps.slogan: Combine the estimates into stability and convergence to an equilibrium.
steps.detail: Given $\varepsilon > 0$, take $\delta' = \min(\delta, \varepsilon/C)$. Then $|x(t)| + |y(t)| \le C\delta' \le \varepsilon$ for all $t \ge 0$, which is [Lyapunov stability](c:lyapunov-stability); the previous step gives convergence to the equilibrium $(0, y_\infty)$.

concepts.c:ordinary-differential-equation: Solutions of the equation are estimated by variation of constants.
concepts.c:eigenvalue: Eigenvalues with negative real part give exponential decay of $e^{At}$.
concepts.c:continuously-differentiable-map: The $C^1$ property gives small Lipschitz bounds near the origin and local solutions.
concepts.c:lyapunov-stability: The estimates give solutions that stay close to the origin for all time.

source.note: Malkin's critical-case theorem (I. G. Malkin, Theory of Stability of Motion, 1952); the proof is the standard variation-of-constants and Gronwall bootstrap.

statement: Consider the spin-$s$ Heisenberg model on a periodic box of $\mathbb{Z}^d$ with $d \in \{1, 2\}$, $H = -\tfrac12\sum_{i \ne j} J(i-j)\,\mathbf{S}_i \cdot \mathbf{S}_j - h\sum_i S_i^z$, where $J(R) = J(-R)$ is real and $\sum_R |J(R)||R|^2 < \infty$. At every temperature $T > 0$, the magnetization per site of the [Gibbs state](c:gibbs-distribution) in the [thermodynamic limit](c:thermodynamic-limit) tends to $0$ as $h \to 0$, so the [continuous symmetry](c:continuous-symmetry) of spin rotations is not broken.

hypotheses.text: The model is the spin-$s$ Heisenberg model above, with [Gibbs state](c:gibbs-distribution) $e^{-\beta H}/Z$ on a periodic box that grows to $\mathbb{Z}^d$.
The dimension is $d = 1$ or $d = 2$.
The coupling is symmetric, real and short range: $J(R) = J(-R)$ and $\sum_R |J(R)||R|^2 < \infty$.
The temperature is positive: $T > 0$, so $\beta = 1/k_BT$ is finite.

conclusion: $\lim_{h \to 0} M(T,h) = 0$ for the magnetization per site $M(T,h) = \langle S_i^z\rangle$ in the thermodynamic limit.

proofs.name: Bogoliubov inequality and a divergent sum
proofs.slogan: The Bogoliubov inequality bounds the spin fluctuations from below by the squared magnetization, and in $d \le 2$ the sum over wave vectors diverges.
proofs.scope: The isotropic Heisenberg model for $h > 0$, the member of the family that Mermin and Wagner treated; the classical XY and $O(N)$ models and general Gibbs states (Dobrushin and Shlosman) are other members, not proved here. The box has $N$ sites and the estimates are uniform in $N$, so the thermodynamic limit is taken afterwards.

roles.why: The spin commutation relations and the bound $|S^\alpha| \le s$ give the two commutators and the sum rule.
In $d \le 2$ the integral of $1/k^2$ near $k = 0$ diverges.
The second moment $\sum_R |J(R)||R|^2$ bounds the double commutator by $bk^2$.
A finite $\beta$ makes the Gibbs state and the Bogoliubov inequality available, and $k_BT > 0$ keeps the bound nontrivial.

steps.slogan: Quote the Bogoliubov inequality for the Gibbs state.
steps.detail: For operators $A$ and $C$ and the Gibbs state at inverse temperature $\beta$, $|\langle [C, A]\rangle|^2 \le \tfrac{\beta}{2}\,\langle \{A, A^\dagger\}\rangle\,\langle [[C, H], C^\dagger]\rangle$, where $[\cdot,\cdot]$ is the [commutator](c:commutator). This is the only external input.

steps.slogan: Choose $C = S_k^+$ and $A = S_{-k}^-$ from the spin Fourier modes.
steps.detail: Let $S_k^\pm = \sum_i e^{-ik\cdot R_i}S_i^\pm$ be the spin [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform). Then $A^\dagger = C$ and $[C, A] = 2\sum_i S_i^z$, so $\langle [C, A]\rangle = 2NM$.

steps.slogan: Bound the double commutator by the field term and the interaction term.
steps.detail: A direct computation gives $\langle [[C,H],C^\dagger]\rangle = 2hNM + \sum_{i,j}J(i-j)\big(1 - \cos k\cdot(R_i - R_j)\big)\langle 2S_i^zS_j^z + S_i^xS_j^x + S_i^yS_j^y\rangle$. With $1 - \cos\theta \le \theta^2/2$ and $|\langle S_i^\alpha S_j^\alpha\rangle| \le s^2$, this is at most $N(2h|M| + bk^2)$ with $b = 2s^2\sum_R|J(R)||R|^2$.

steps.slogan: Insert the estimates to bound the fluctuation of each wave vector from below.
steps.detail: The Bogoliubov inequality gives $4N^2M^2 \le \tfrac{\beta}{2}\,\langle \{A_k, A_k^\dagger\}\rangle\,N(2h|M| + bk^2)$. So $\langle \{A_k, A_k^\dagger\}\rangle \ge 8NM^2k_BT/(2h|M| + bk^2)$ for every wave vector $k$.

steps.slogan: Sum over the wave vectors and use the sum rule for spin length.
steps.detail: Since $\sum_k e^{ik\cdot(R_j - R_i)} = N\delta_{ij}$, we get $\sum_k \langle\{A_k, A_k^\dagger\}\rangle = N\sum_i \langle 2(S_i^x)^2 + 2(S_i^y)^2\rangle \le 2N^2s(s+1)$. Hence $s(s+1) \ge 4M^2k_BT\,\tfrac1N\sum_k (2h|M| + bk^2)^{-1}$.

steps.slogan: Let $N \to \infty$ and then $h \to 0$ to force $M$ to zero.
steps.detail: The average over $k$ becomes $(2\pi)^{-d}\int d^dk\,(2h|M| + bk^2)^{-1}$, which is at least the same integral with $|M|$ replaced by $s$. This tends to infinity as $h \to 0$ when $d \le 2$, so $M^2 \le s(s+1)/(4k_BT \cdot \text{integral}) \to 0$.

concepts.c:gibbs-distribution: The Bogoliubov inequality holds in the Gibbs state at inverse temperature $\beta$.
concepts.c:thermodynamic-limit: The estimates are uniform in the box size, so they pass to the thermodynamic limit.
concepts.c:continuous-symmetry: The rotation symmetry of the spins is the continuous symmetry that cannot break.
concepts.c:commutator: The inequality and the two choices of operators are built from commutators.
concepts.c:fourier-transform: Fourier modes of the spins turn the double commutator into a function of $k$.

source.ref: N. D. Mermin and H. Wagner, Absence of ferromagnetism or antiferromagnetism in one- or two-dimensional isotropic Heisenberg models, Physical Review Letters 17 (1966), 1133-1136
source.note: The steps follow the published proof; the Bogoliubov inequality of the first step is quoted.
